Again, probabilities are a complex subject and many people don't really grasp them. If you have a 1:100 chance of success with each singular event, and the probabilities aren't changed each time, then you have the same odds of success on the 100th try than you do on the first. (With some margin for error and few things are ever without assuming some spherical cows.)

For example, a digital slot machine may have a 1:100 chance of winning - but the gaming commission also adds the caveat that it must pay out 1:100 times.

At the same time, anyone familiar with the Martingale Method of betting will also be familiar with how very long one can go without winning.

Percentage vs raw changes is a big one.

Another that I see people misunderstand is independent events. I keep hearing "we havent had a big hurricane in a few years so we're overdue for one". Each hurricane season is essentially a completely different event. Obviously sea surface temperatures and other factors play a role, but being hit by a hurricane one season won't make you any safer for the next year.

If a person flips tails 5 times in a row, most people think that they're "overdue" for a heads... in reality every throw is 50/50 --- none of the previous flips matter.

On that note, all of introductory probability ("disjoint events, mutual exclusivity, etc) seems to be poorly understood by most.

Some seemingly ordinary games of chance have such a high volatility that they don't have an expected value.

For instance, there's a backgammon position where the next player to roll a 6 has a very high probability of winning. This clearly favors the player who rolls the dice next, and by enough that he should double the stakes if allowed, but not by so much that the opponent should refuse the double and concede the game.

So he doubles and rolls the dice. 11/36 times he wins, but the other 25/36 times, the roles reverse and his opponent has control. She doubles right back and rolls her dice, and the doubling continues until somebody rolls a 6.

Go ahead, try to compute the expected value: 2(11/36) - 4(11/36)(25/36) + 8(11/36)(25/36)^2 - 16(11/36)(25/36)^3 + ... It's an infinite geometric series, but the ratio is -50/36 so it doesn't converge.

How can we compute the equity for other backgammon positions if there are monsters like this lurking in the background?
